content.title: What are Eid Holidays? | Facts for Kids | Twinkl - Twinkl
content.text: Eid is an Islamic festival founded by the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). We tend to think of Eid as being one celebration, but it’s an umbrella term for two religious events which follow Ramadan. Eid Holidays – Information for Kids The Eid holidays are very important events in the Islamic calendar. They're also super topics to use when teaching your children about different religious holidays. Keep on reading to find out all about the holidays, when they are, and how they’re celebrated. What are the two Eid holidays? Many people think that Eid is one holiday, but this is not the case. There are two holidays that are collectively called Eid, each with its own rituals and celebrations. The two individual Eid holidays are as follows: Eid Al-Fitr: This holiday marks the end of fasting during Ramadan.Eid Al-Adha: This holiday honours Prophet Ibrahim’s (PBUH) dedication to Allah. It also coincides with the Hajj, a pilgrimage made by Muslim people to Mecca. If you’d like to wish somebody a blessed Eid, the phrase used is ‘Eid Mubarak’. This phrase can be used for both of the Eid holidays, but if you want to be more specific, you can say ‘Eid Al-Fitr Mubarak’ or ‘Eid Al-Adha Mubarak’. Teaching Wiki Contents What is Eid Al-Fitr? When is Eid Al-Fitr? How is Eid Al-Fitr Celebrated? What is Eid Al-Adha? When is Eid Al-Adha? How is Eid Al-Adha Celebrated? Eid Al-Fitr Eid Al-Fitr is the first Eid holiday. It’s the smaller of the two, only lasting for one day. What is Eid Al-Fitr? Eid Al-Fitr is the first of the two Eid holidays, and it is the feast of fast-breaking. It marks the end of Ramadan, a time when Muslim people fast from before dawn until after sunset. When people take part in a fast, they don’t eat or drink for a certain amount of time. In the case of Ramadan, people fast so that they can strengthen their bond with Allah. Ramadan is the name given to the ninth month in the Islamic calendar. It’s believed that Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) had the earliest verses of the Qu’ran revealed to him during this month. Muslim people fast throughout Ramadan, as well as spend time reciting the Qu’ran. They’re also encouraged to show kindness and patience, and give to charity. When is Eid Al-Fitr? Eid Al-Fitr is an annual holiday that officially takes place on the first day of Shawwal, the 10th month of the Islamic calendar. This calendar, called the Hijri calendar, is a lunar calendar. This means that it’s around 11 days shorter than the solar calendar that is often used in day-to-day life. Due to this discrepancy between the number of days in a year, Eid Al-Fitr takes place on different dates of the solar calendar every year, around eleven days earlier than the previous year. The holiday doesn’t start until the new moon has been seen. This means that Eid Al-Fitr starts at a different time for most people, depending on where in the world they live. Some Muslim people start celebrating Eid Al-Fitr when the new moon is seen in Mecca. How is Eid Al-Fitr celebrated? Eid Al-Fitr is celebrated in a range of ways. A prayer service is held for the community, which often attracts a large number of people. Even Muslim people who don’t usually attend prayer services will come along. When attending this service, people make an effort to wear their best clothes. There is also a feeling of friendliness and kindness, with people putting their troubles to one side in order to celebrate. Families and friends will meet up together to spend time with one another and exchange gifts. The feast held on Eid Al-Fitr contains lots of sweet treats and desserts – in fact, the feast is sometimes called the Sugar Feast. Different countries have their own favourite foods that they eat. In Turkey, baklava and Turkish delight are very popular as gifts. People in Iraq and Saudi Arabia will bake and eat kleichas, rose-flavoured biscuits with a date and nut filling. In Morocco, a sweet filo pastry parcel called briouat is a commonly eaten dish. Eid Al-Fitr is also a time for Muslim people to give back to their communities. Before the Eid prayer, self-supporting adults who have food beyond their needs pay Zakat Al-Fitr (sometimes called Fitrana). Zakat is one of the five pillars of Islam, meaning this donation is compulsory, and is used to support those in need. Eid Al-Adha Eid Al-Adha, the second of the Eid holidays, is a bigger holiday than Eid Al-Fitr. It can last for up to four days, depending on where you’re celebrating. What is Eid Al-Adha? Eid Al-Adha, the Feast of Sacrifice, is a holiday celebrating two things. It primarily honours the sacrifice that Prophet Ibrahim (PBUH) was willing to make to Allah. Allah spoke to Prophet Ibrahim (PBUH), asking him to sacrifice his son, Ismail. Just as Prophet Ibrahim (PBUH) was about to sacrifice his son, Allah replaced him with a ram. Eid Al-Adha gives Muslim people the chance to revere Prophet Ibrahim’s (PBUH) obedience and devotion to Allah. The holiday also coincides with the Hajj, an annual pilgrimage to Mecca that millions of Muslim people take part in every year. Whilst the Hajj has no direct connection to Eid Al-Adha, the two are often celebrated together as they happen at the same time. When is Eid Al-Adha? Eid Al-Adha starts on the tenth day of the final month in the Hijri calendar. This is two months after Eid Al-Fitr, and it can last up to four days. Just like Eid Al-Fitr, the date of Eid Al-Adha is based on the Hijri calendar, which is a lunar calendar. This means that the date of Eid Al-Adha on the solar calendar changes by around eleven days every year. How is Eid Al-Adha celebrated? In predominantly Muslim countries, Eid Al-Adha is a public holiday. This means that people have time off work and school to celebrate. At the start of Eid Al-Adha, Muslim people will perform ghusl, which is a purification ritual. They’ll then wear their best clothes and go to the mosque for a prayer service. The main element of Eid Al-Adha is Qurbani. Qurbani is the sacrifice of an animal in the name of Allah. Before Qurbani can happen, Eid Salah (Eid prayers) are said in the morning at the mosque in front of the congregation. The act of Qurbani can be traced back to the time of Prophet Ibrahim (PBUH) when he was asked by Allah to sacrifice his son. Every year, Muslim families who can afford it take part in Qurbani, where an animal like a sheep, goat, or cow is sacrificed in a Halal way. Once the animal has been sacrificed, it’s separated into three sections. A third of the animal is kept for family, another is for friends, and the final third is donated to those in need. Unlike Eid Al-Fitr, whose feast is known for its sweets, the feast on Eid Al-Adha is predominantly savoury. The food eaten usually depends on the animal sacrificed. For example, if a cow has been sacrificed, then the feast will include beef. The meat is cooked in a number of ways, and the most popular dishes are kebabs, biryani, and haleem, which is a stew that includes meat, lentils and wheat.
